title: Building TurboTax
subtitle: From one W-2 to ten million returns on April 15
description: Follow a tax-filing app as it grows from helping one person file a simple federal return into a full product: a guided interview that adapts to each filer, an engine that hunts for every deduction, official PDF forms, e-filing into government systems that are slow and sometimes offline, a vault for years of sensitive data, payments in and refunds out — and finally the horizontal scaling that keeps it all standing in the final hours before the deadline.

stages.title: One Filer, One W-2

narrative.setup: You're building a tax app for the simplest possible case: a single person with one W-2 from one employer, taking the standard deduction. They create an account, answer a few questions, your app does the arithmetic, and they file a federal return. That's the whole product.

blocks.content:
Your tax app is live. A user creates an account, logs in, types in the numbers from their W-2 (wages, federal tax withheld), confirms they're taking the standard deduction, and your app calculates what they owe or what refund they get back.

The shape is the same [[glossary:client-server|client-server model]] every app uses. The browser is the **client**, your **[[node:server|server]]** runs the tax math, and a **[[node:database|database]]** stores the return so the user can come back and finish it later.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: a paper worksheet
blocks.content: Think of your app as a smart version of the IRS paper worksheet. **The client** is the person holding the pen. **The server** is the worksheet's instructions — "take line 1, subtract line 4, look up the result in the tax table." **The database** is the filing cabinet where the finished worksheet gets stored. At this scale, one worksheet and one drawer is all you need.

A return isn't a single action — it's a session that spans days. Someone starts on Monday, hunts for a document, and comes back Thursday to finish. So the server has to save the half-finished return as **[[glossary:state|state]]** in the database after every step.

1. User enters their wages — the server saves it to the database
2. User comes back later — the server loads the saved return
3. User hits **File** — the server runs the final calculation and records the result

Everything the user types has to survive them closing the laptop.

There's one thing you can't skip even on day one: **identity**. A tax return is built out of the most sensitive data a person has — their Social Security number, their income, their dependents. You can't let just anyone open it, and you can't let the wrong person see it.

So before any of the tax flow, the user signs in. A small **[[node:auth|login]]** step checks their password, hands the browser a session, and from then on every request carries proof of who they are. The return they're editing is tied to that identity, and the database stores it as **[[glossary:persistence|persisted]]**, protected data — not a public document.

blocks.caption: The whole product: a login gate, a server that does the tax math, and a database that remembers the return

blocks.content: Tax software is different from most apps in two important ways. First, being fast matters less than being **correct** — a chat app that drops a message is annoying, but a tax app that miscalculates a return creates a legal problem for the user. Second, the data is uniquely **sensitive** — a leaked draft message is embarrassing, a leaked return is identity theft. Correctness and confidentiality are the product, and both start on day one.

At this stage, resist the urge to build for fifty states and every edge case. A single-W-2, standard-deduction return covers a huge share of real filers. Ship the simple case, get real returns flowing, and let actual users tell you which complications to handle next. The login can stay simple too — one email and password — as long as the data behind it is treated as sensitive from the start.

blocks.decision: Should the tax calculation run in the browser or on the server?

options.name: In the browser
pros: Instant feedback as the user types
No server load for the math
cons: The logic is exposed and can be tampered with
Users run whatever version they last loaded
You can't trust the number it produces

options.name: On the server
pros: One authoritative, trusted result
Fix a rule once and everyone gets it
The filed number can't be forged
cons: A round-trip for each calculation
The server carries the compute cost

blocks.choice: Run the authoritative calculation on the server. For tax software the filed number carries legal weight, so it has to be **trusted and consistent** — you can't let the client decide what someone owes. Many apps still run a lightweight copy in the browser for a snappy live estimate, but the number that actually gets filed is always the server's.

blocks.question: A user fills in half their return, closes the browser, and comes back two days later. What has to be true for their progress to still be there?

options.text: The browser kept the numbers in memory while it was closed
options.explanation: A closed browser keeps nothing. Anything held only in the browser or in the server's memory is gone the moment either one restarts.

options.text: The server saved the in-progress return to the database, tied to the user's identity, as they went
options.explanation: Because a return is a multi-day session, the server has to persist each step to the database under the signed-in user's identity. When they log back in, the server reloads that saved state and they pick up where they left off.

options.text: Nothing — they'll have to start over every visit
options.explanation: That would make the product unusable. Saving progress is the entire reason the database exists in this design.

suggestedQuestions: Where exactly does the tax calculation happen — the browser or the server?
Why does a tax app need login on day one when other apps add it later?
What does it mean to 'save state' for a tax return?

stages.title: The Guided Interview

narrative.setup: Word spreads and your users get more complicated. Now they itemize deductions, report freelance income, sell stock, and — the big one — earn money in more than one state. Someone who lives in New Jersey but works in New York has to file three returns: federal, NJ, and NY, each with its own rules. They don't know any of that. Your job is to ask the right questions and quietly do the hard part.
narrative.problem: Two things break at once. First, you can't show everyone the same form anymore — the questions a freelancer needs are useless to a retiree, and asking all of them would drown every user. Second, your clean little calculation has turned into a tangle of federal rules, fifty state rule sets, and dozens of income types jammed into one server. And there's a quieter failure: users are overpaying, because they don't know which deductions and credits they qualify for, and your app never tells them.
narrative.resolution: You split the brain into three parts. A workflow engine drives a dynamic interview, deciding which question to ask next based on what the user has already said. A dedicated calculation engine holds each jurisdiction's rules as its own module. And a recommendation engine scans the return for every deduction and credit the filer qualifies for, optimizing for the largest legal refund.

blocks.content:
The first thing that breaks is the interview itself. A single hardcoded form can't serve a freelancer with stock sales and a retiree with one pension — show everyone every question and you bury them; show everyone too few and you miss income.

What you actually need is a flow that **branches**. "Did you have any income other than a W-2?" If no, skip eleven screens. If yes, "Was any of it self-employment?" — and now a whole sub-interview about business expenses opens up. The path through the app is different for every filer.

So you build a **[[node:workflow|workflow engine]]**: a separate service that owns the decision of *what comes next*. The browser stops being in charge of the flow. Instead it asks the engine, "given everything this user has told me so far, what's the next screen?" The engine consults the rules, looks at the answers, and replies with the next question — or with "you're done."

This is the key inversion: the front end becomes a **thin renderer**. It doesn't know the tax interview; it just draws whatever the workflow engine tells it to draw. The logic of the interview lives in one place you can change without touching the UI.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: a great accountant's follow-up questions
blocks.content: A bad tax preparer hands you a 40-page form and says "fill in everything that applies." A great one asks one question at a time and *listens*: "Any kids? — Okay, how old? — Did you pay for childcare?" Each answer decides the next question. The **workflow engine** is that great preparer's instinct, encoded. The screen in front of you is just the preparer's mouth — it says whatever the brain decides to ask next. Change how the brain thinks, and every conversation changes, without retraining the mouth.

The second thing that breaks is the math. A multi-state return is really several returns that share data: your New-Jersey-resident-working-in-New-York user needs a federal return, a New York non-resident return, and a New Jersey resident return that credits the tax already paid to New York. Each has different brackets, different deductions, different forms.

Cramming federal logic, fifty state rule sets, and every income type into one server becomes unmaintainable fast. So you pull the math out into a dedicated **[[node:calc-engine|calculation engine]]** where federal and each state's rules live as independent modules. This is a step toward [[glossary:microservices|microservices]]: when New York changes its brackets, you update the New York module and nothing else — the federal logic and the other 49 states are untouched.

The third problem is the one users can't see: they're leaving money on the table. Someone with a side gig might not know that a home-office deduction, mileage, or the Earned Income Tax Credit applies to them. A plain calculator computes whatever they enter and stops there.

So you add a **[[node:recommender|refund optimizer]]** — a recommendation engine that looks at the whole return and asks, "what is this person eligible for that they haven't claimed?" It surfaces deductions and credits, models the impact of each, and steers the interview toward the combination that produces the **largest legal refund**. This is the "maximize your refund" promise, and it's a distinct piece of logic from the calculation engine: the calc engine answers *what is the tax given these inputs*, the optimizer answers *which inputs are we missing*.

blocks.caption: The app server delegates to three specialists: a workflow engine that drives the interview, a calc engine that does the math, and a refund optimizer that hunts for deductions

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: specialist accountants
blocks.content: At first you were the sole accountant doing everything. Now you've hired specialists. The **app server** is the office manager who greets the client and routes the work. The **workflow engine** is the intake specialist who knows exactly which question to ask next. The **calculation engine** is the room of rule experts, each fluent in one rulebook. And the **refund optimizer** is the seasoned advisor who glances at your file and says "wait — you never claimed the childcare credit." Each is an expert in exactly one job, so improving one doesn't risk breaking the others.

blocks.decision: Should the interview flow be hardcoded in the front end, or driven by a separate workflow engine?

options.name: Hardcoded in the UI
pros: Simple for a handful of screens
No extra service to run
Fast — no round-trip to ask what's next
cons: Every tax-law change means a UI redeploy
Logic gets copy-pasted across web and mobile
Impossible to test the flow on its own

options.name: A workflow engine drives it
pros: One source of truth for the interview
Web and mobile render the same flow
Change the questions without shipping a new app
The flow can be tested in isolation
cons: Another service to build and run
The UI must ask the engine what to show next

blocks.choice: Drive the interview from a workflow engine. Tax rules change every year and the same flow has to run identically on web and mobile, so the interview logic can't live baked into one client. Centralizing it lets you update questions as laws change without redeploying the apps, and lets you test the entire flow as data. The cost is a real one — the UI now leans on the engine to tell it what to show — but it's the same trade that put the calculation on the server in Stage 1: keep the authoritative logic in one place you control.

blocks.content: Notice the pattern across all three services: the front end keeps getting thinner. The workflow engine decides *what to ask*, the calc engine decides *what it adds up to*, the optimizer decides *what to suggest* — and the browser just renders the answers. When the interface is a thin shell over engines you control, you can change the product's behavior for millions of users without anyone installing an update.

blocks.question: Why move the interview's branching logic into a workflow engine instead of coding it into the front-end screens?

options.text: It makes the screens render faster
options.explanation: It usually adds a round-trip, not removes one. The win isn't speed — it's having one authoritative copy of the interview logic.

options.text: So the interview is defined once and can change with tax law without redeploying the web and mobile apps, and can be tested on its own
options.explanation: The flow is the part of a tax app that changes most — every year, and per jurisdiction. Centralizing it in an engine means one update covers every client, and the branching can be tested as data instead of by clicking through screens.

options.text: Front-end code can't express if/else branching
options.explanation: It absolutely can. The problem isn't capability — it's that hardcoding the flow scatters tax logic across clients and ties every rule change to an app release.

blocks.label: Deep dive: why three engines instead of one big service
blocks.content:
You could keep piling logic into the app server. The reason to split it into a workflow engine, a calculation engine, and a refund optimizer comes down to forces specific to tax software:

**They change on different schedules.** The interview flow changes when the product team rewords questions. The calculation rules change when Congress and fifty legislatures change the law. The optimizer changes when you discover a credit you weren't surfacing. Separating them means each can evolve without retesting the others.

**The calc engine gets reused everywhere.** The live refund meter as the user types, the optimizer's "what if you claimed this" simulations, and the final filed return must all run through the *exact same* calculation logic. A separate engine guarantees the preview and the filed return can never disagree.

**Each can be tested in isolation.** A calculation engine with clean inputs and outputs can be run against thousands of known-correct returns automatically. That regression suite is how you sleep at night during tax season — you can prove a code change didn't alter any result it shouldn't have.

suggestedQuestions: How does the workflow engine decide which question to show next?
Why keep the calculation engine and the refund optimizer separate — don't they both do tax math?
How can the live estimate and the filed return be guaranteed to match?

stages.title: Producing and Filing the Return

narrative.setup: The numbers are right and the optimizer has found every credit. Now comes the part the user actually came for: turning their answers into an official return and getting it into the government's hands. That sounds simple. It is not.
narrative.problem: A tax return isn't a row in your database — it's specific government forms, filled out exactly, that the user needs a copy of and the IRS needs transmitted. Worse, the systems you transmit to are slow, rate-limited, occasionally down for maintenance, and — for some states and forms — don't offer an electronic interface at all. If your server waits on the IRS before confirming, users stare at spinners and hit errors during the busiest hours. And nobody is telling the user what happened after they clicked File.
narrative.resolution: A PDF service renders the official forms — both the copy the filer keeps and the document that gets transmitted. Filing goes through a queue and a background worker that submits to, and retrieves acknowledgements from, the government APIs, retrying when they're slow. When an API is down or doesn't exist, the worker falls back to a durable store of the computed return and either retries later or produces a paper return to mail. And an email service keeps the filer informed at every step.

blocks.content:
First, you have to **produce the document**. Behind the friendly interview, a tax return is a precise set of government forms — a 1040 with its schedules, each state's forms — that must be filled out to the line. The user wants a copy they can save, print, or show a lender. And the electronic transmission to the IRS is itself built from a structured rendering of those same forms.

So you add a **[[node:pdf|PDF service]]**: it takes the finished, calculated return and renders the exact official forms — pixel-correct, every line in the right box. One job, done in one place, used both for the filer's record copy and as the source for what gets transmitted.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the print shop with the official stencils
blocks.content: Your interview is a friendly conversation; the IRS only accepts answers on its own rigid forms. The **PDF service** is the back-office print shop that owns the official stencils. You hand it the finished numbers; it stamps them onto the exact government forms, identical every time. Keeping it as one service means there's a single place that knows what a valid 1040 looks like — when the form changes next year, you re-cut one stencil, not a dozen.

Now the hard part: **filing**. When a user hits File, you have to transmit their return to the IRS and to each state agency through their [[glossary:api|e-file APIs]]. These government systems are slow, rate-limited, and occasionally down for maintenance. If your server waits for the IRS to respond before showing a confirmation, the user stares at a spinner for 40 seconds — or sees an error when the IRS is overloaded.

So you stop waiting. The File request drops a job onto a **[[glossary:message-queue|queue]]**, and the app instantly tells the user "Your return has been submitted — we'll email you when it's accepted." A **[[node:efile-worker|background worker]]** pulls jobs off the queue and does the slow, unreliable work out of the user's sight. This is [[glossary:async|asynchronous]] processing, and it buys you three things: the user isn't blocked, [[glossary:retry|retries]] happen automatically when the IRS is down, and you submit at whatever rate the government will accept.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the post office counter
blocks.content: Filing synchronously is like mailing a certified letter and refusing to leave the post office counter until the recipient signs for it — you'd be standing there for days. Filing through a queue is how it actually works: you hand the letter to the clerk, get a tracking number, and walk away. The **background worker** is the postal system that delivers it, retries if the address is busy, and notifies you when it's signed for.

The government APIs aren't a one-way chute, either. The worker doesn't just **submit** — it also **retrieves**: the prior-year income figure used to verify identity, an Identity Protection PIN, and most importantly the **acknowledgement** that comes back hours later saying the return was accepted or rejected. Filing is a conversation with a system on the other side, not a fire-and-forget.

But what about when the government system is simply *unavailable* — down for a maintenance window, or, for certain states and forms, offering no electronic interface at all? You can't lose the return, and you can't make the user wait for a system that won't answer.

So the worker has a **[[node:fallback-store|fallback path]]**. The fully computed return — every number, every form, the exact tax owed or refunded — is written to a durable store the moment it's ready, independent of whether the API is reachable. If the API is merely down, the worker retries from that store on its own schedule until it gets through. If a jurisdiction has no e-file API at all, the system falls back to generating a **paper return** (another job for the PDF service) for the filer to print and mail. Either way, the calculated result is preserved and the filing eventually completes — the unreliable external system never becomes a single point of data loss.

blocks.caption: The return becomes official documents and reaches the government: a PDF service renders the forms, a queue and worker submit and retrieve through the e-file APIs, a fallback store guards against outages, and an email service keeps the filer informed

blocks.content:
Finally, somebody has to keep the user in the loop. Because filing is asynchronous, the moment of "done" is split across hours: submitted now, accepted (or rejected) later. The user has closed the laptop. So you add an **[[node:email|email service]]** — a dedicated channel that sends the submission receipt, the acceptance confirmation, and, if the IRS bounces the return, a clear explanation of what to fix.

Making email its own service (rather than something the worker does inline) matters: sending mail is itself a slow, sometimes-failing external call, and you don't want a flaky mail provider to stall the filing pipeline. The worker hands off a "notify this user" job and moves on.

Asynchronous filing changes what "done" means. **Submitted is not the same as accepted.** The IRS can reject a return hours later — a mismatched name, a duplicate Social Security number, a wrong prior-year figure. Your system has to track every return through submitted, accepted, or rejected, and tell the user clearly which state it's in. "I clicked File" is not the same as "the government has my return," and the email service is how you close that gap honestly.

blocks.decision: When a user clicks File, submit to the IRS right then, or hand it to a queue?

options.name: Submit synchronously
pros: The user gets a real accepted/rejected answer on the spot
Nothing extra to build
cons: User waits on a slow government system
Errors out when the IRS is overloaded or down
A filing surge has nowhere to go
No graceful path when an API is unavailable

options.name: Queue + background worker
pros: Instant acknowledgement to the user
Automatic retries when the IRS is down
You submit at whatever rate it accepts
A natural place to fall back to a durable store
cons: 'Submitted' no longer means 'accepted'
You must track and surface each return's status

blocks.choice: Put filings on a queue. The IRS and state systems are slow and sometimes offline, so blocking a user on them is a bad trade — far better to acknowledge instantly and let a worker push the return through with retries, falling back to a durable store when an API is down. The price is real: you now have to track every return through submitted to accepted or rejected, and tell the user plainly where it stands.

blocks.scenario: A user files their return at 9:00 PM. The worker submits it to the IRS, but the IRS system is down for maintenance and the request fails. At 9:01 PM the worker retries and it fails again. The user, seeing nothing happen, clicks File a second time, dropping another job on the queue for the same return.
blocks.question: How do you keep this from submitting the same return to the IRS twice once the system comes back up?

options.text: Give each return a unique filing ID and have the worker check 'has this return already been accepted or in flight?' before every submission
options.explanation: This makes submission idempotent: no matter how many times the job runs, the return reaches the IRS at most once. The worker keys on the return's filing ID and refuses to submit one that's already in flight or accepted. Double-filing a tax return is a serious problem, so this guard is essential.

options.text: Remove the retry logic so a failed submission never tries again
options.explanation: That trades one problem for a worse one. Without retries, every return filed during the IRS maintenance window would silently fail and never reach the government at all.

options.text: Disable the File button for 10 minutes after the first click
options.explanation: A UI delay might reduce duplicate clicks, but it doesn't prevent them — and it does nothing about the worker's own retries. Correctness has to be guaranteed in the system, not in the button.

suggestedQuestions: Why render PDFs at all instead of just sending the IRS the raw numbers?
What happens to a return if a state's e-file system has no API?
Why make email its own service instead of having the worker send mail directly?

stages.title: Identity and Money

narrative.setup: You now hold years of returns for millions of people — Social Security numbers, every dollar of income, dependents, bank accounts. You also charge a fee to file, and you route refunds. This stage isn't about a new feature; it's about the two things that, done wrong, end the company: the sensitive data you guard, and the money that moves through you.
narrative.problem: A single password is a thin gate on a vault of identity data, and attackers know tax accounts are gold. Users also hate re-typing — they want to sign in with accounts they already have and import their W-2 without copying numbers by hand. And once a return is filed, money has to move in two directions: your fee in, the government's refund out — without you ever quietly sitting on funds you shouldn't.
narrative.resolution: You add real authentication: single sign-on and OAuth so users bring existing identities and authorize data imports, plus a second factor for accounts that hold this much PII. You move the most sensitive data into an isolated, encrypted vault separate from the app database. A payment service collects the filing fee. And a bank integration disperses the refund — including the option to deduct your fee straight from it.

blocks.content:
In Stage 1 a password was enough to protect one draft return. Now the same login opens **years** of filed returns, Social Security numbers, and bank details for millions of people. That makes your accounts a prime target, and a password alone — reused, phished, or guessed — is far too thin a gate.

So authentication grows up. The **[[node:auth|auth service]]** becomes its own component, responsible for proving who someone is before the app server trusts a single request — and for doing it in more than one way.

First, you stop forcing everyone to invent a new password. With **single sign-on (SSO)** and **OAuth**, a user can "Sign in with Google" or Apple: they prove their identity to a provider they already trust, and that provider vouches for them to you. You never see their Google password — you receive a signed token that says "this is really them."

OAuth does double duty here. Beyond login, it's how you let a user **import data without handing over passwords**. "Connect your payroll provider to import your W-2" works by the user authorizing your app, at the provider, to read just that one document — a scoped, revocable grant. The provider hands you a limited access token, never the user's credentials.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the valet key
blocks.content: A modern car comes with a valet key that opens the door and starts the engine but won't unlock the glovebox or the trunk. **OAuth** is that valet key. When you "connect your payroll to import your W-2," you hand TurboTax a valet key to your payroll account — enough to read this year's W-2, nothing more — and you can take the key back anytime. You never give them the master key (your password). **SSO** is the flip side: instead of cutting a new key for every shop you visit, you carry one trusted key (your Google identity) that the shops agree to honor.

Second, you add a **second factor (2FA)**. A password is something you *know*; a second factor is something you *have* — a code from an authenticator app, a prompt on your phone, a hardware key. Requiring both means a stolen password isn't enough to open someone's tax history.

For a vault of this sensitivity, 2FA isn't a nice-to-have — it's the difference between "an attacker who phishes one password reads everything" and "a phished password is useless on its own." The auth service is where you enforce it, stepping up to the second factor on login, on sensitive changes, and on logins from new devices.

Now the data itself. Not all of it is equally sensitive: a user's interview progress is ordinary app data, but their Social Security number and the bank account their refund lands in are the crown jewels. Keeping the crown jewels in the same table as everything else means one mistake exposes everything.

So you carve out a **[[node:pii-vault|PII vault]]** — an isolated, heavily-restricted store for the most sensitive fields, encrypted at rest, reachable only through a narrow interface, with its own tight access controls and audit logging. The app database holds a token in place of the real SSN; only the vault can turn that token back into the number, and only for the few operations that genuinely need it. Shrinking the blast radius like this is the whole game with PII.

Then there's the money, moving in two directions. **In:** you charge a fee to file, so you add a **[[node:payment|payment service]]** (think Stripe) that collects the card payment, handles the sensitive card data so it never touches your servers, and tells the app when the charge succeeds. **Out:** once the IRS issues a refund, it has to reach the filer. A **[[node:bank|bank / ACH integration]]** routes that refund to the user's bank account, and powers the popular "pay with your refund" option — your fee is deducted from the refund before the rest is deposited, so the user pays nothing up front.

The rule with both directions is the same: be a conduit, not a reservoir. You move money promptly and visibly; you never quietly hold funds that belong to the user or the government.

blocks.caption: The trust layer: an auth service backed by SSO/OAuth providers and 2FA, an isolated encrypted PII vault, a payment service collecting the fee, and a bank integration dispersing the refund

blocks.decision: Build authentication and payments in-house, or lean on specialized providers?

options.name: Build it yourself
pros: Total control over the experience
No third-party fees
No external dependency
cons: You become responsible for storing passwords and card data securely
You inherit a huge compliance and attack surface
Years of work to match what providers do by default

options.name: Use SSO/OAuth providers and a payment processor
pros: Card data and federated identity never touch your servers
Compliance (PCI, etc.) is largely the provider's burden
Battle-tested security you couldn't build alone
Faster to ship
cons: Per-transaction and per-identity costs
You depend on their uptime and policies
Less control over edge cases

blocks.choice: Lean on providers for the parts where a mistake is catastrophic. The safest credit-card data is the data you never store; the safest password is the one a federated identity provider holds instead of you. Offloading card handling to a payment processor and identity to SSO/OAuth shrinks both your attack surface and your compliance burden enormously. You still own the PII vault yourself — the tax data *is* your product — but you encrypt and isolate it rather than treating it like ordinary rows. The cost is real dependency and per-transaction fees, and it's the right trade when the downside of doing it yourself is a breach.

blocks.content: Identity and money have the largest blast radius in the whole system. A bug that shows the wrong refund estimate is embarrassing; a bug that leaks a vault of SSNs or misroutes a refund is existential. Treat these components differently from the rest: least-privilege access, encryption at rest, audit logging on every read of the vault, and a hard rule that sensitive card data and federated passwords never get stored by you at all.

blocks.scenario: An attacker phishes a user's password and logs in from a new device, hoping to download three years of filed returns — full of Social Security numbers and bank details.
blocks.question: Which design choices, working together, keep this from becoming a full breach of that user's data?

options.text: Require a second factor on the new-device login, and keep SSNs in the isolated, encrypted PII vault behind their own access controls — so a phished password alone unlocks neither the account nor the raw sensitive data
options.explanation: Defense in depth: 2FA means the stolen password isn't enough to get in, and even an authenticated session can't pull raw SSNs out of the vault without passing its separate, tightly-scoped access controls. Each layer shrinks the blast radius of the one in front of it failing.

options.text: Email the user a warning after the attacker has already downloaded the returns
options.explanation: A notification after the fact is good practice, but it's detection, not prevention. By the time the email goes out, the data is gone. The protection has to stop the access, not just report it.

options.text: Force everyone to change their password every 30 days
options.explanation: Frequent forced rotation tends to push users toward weaker, reused passwords and does nothing against a password phished today. A second factor and an isolated vault address the actual attack; a rotation policy doesn't.

suggestedQuestions: How does 'Sign in with Google' let me in without you ever seeing my Google password?
Why store SSNs in a separate vault instead of just encrypting the main database?
How does 'pay with your refund' work without TurboTax holding my money?

stages.title: April 15, 11:59 PM

narrative.setup: It's the night of the deadline. Tax filing isn't steady traffic — it's a wall. Most of the year is quiet, then a huge share of all returns arrive in the final week, and a startling number in the final hour before midnight on April 15. Ten million people are logged in at once, all doing math-heavy work, all running through the interview, the engines, the PDF service, payments — and all trying to file before the clock runs out.
narrative.problem: Your single app server and single calculation engine, fine for a normal Tuesday, are buried. Response times climb to 30 seconds. The calculation engine is pinned at 100% CPU recomputing the same federal brackets for millions of returns. The database is drowning because every keystroke in the interview triggers a save and a reload. Some users get errors at 11:55 PM — and a return filed one minute after midnight can mean penalties.
narrative.resolution: You put a load balancer in front of many identical app servers and engines, scaling out horizontally. You cache the tax rules and bracket tables that every return shares. You add a read replica so all those progress-reloads stop hammering the primary database. And you add rate limiting to keep bots and runaway retries from stealing capacity from real filers.

blocks.content:
Tax season is the hardest kind of load: a sharp, predictable spike. One server — even with your clean engines and queue — can't absorb ten million simultaneous filers. One machine has a ceiling on CPU, memory, and connections.

The answer is [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]]: run many identical app servers and many calculation engines side by side, instead of trying to build one impossibly large machine. Everything you built in the last three stages — the workflow engine, the calc engine, the optimizer, the PDF service — gets replicated across the fleet.

blocks.decision: Deadline night is a wall of traffic. How do you stand up enough capacity?

options.name: One giant machine (vertical)
pros: No architectural changes
Nothing to coordinate across servers
cons: A hard ceiling you eventually hit
A single point of failure on the biggest night
Paid for year-round, used a few weeks

options.name: Many machines (horizontal)
pros: Add as much capacity as the night needs
One server dying doesn't take the site down
cons: Servers must hold no local state
Needs a load balancer and capacity planning

blocks.choice: Scale horizontally, and **pre-provision** the fleet ahead of April 15 rather than autoscaling into the spike — a wall of traffic arrives faster than new machines can boot. Tear it down afterward so you aren't paying for peak capacity in July. The cost you take on is designing every server to be stateless, so any of them can handle any request.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: opening more tax offices
blocks.content: On April 15 you don't make your one accountant work a thousand times faster — that's impossible. You open a hundred identical offices, each fully staffed, and a dispatcher out front sends each arriving client to whichever office has a free desk. Every office follows the same rulebook, so it doesn't matter which one you walk into. That dispatcher is a load balancer.

A [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] sits in front of your fleet and spreads incoming requests across all the [[node:server|app servers]]. If one server crashes under the strain, the load balancer's health checks notice and route around it. The user just sees turbotax.com — they have no idea there are two hundred servers behind it.

The calculation engines scale out the same way, so the heavy tax math runs in parallel across many machines.

blocks.caption: The deadline-night architecture: a load balancer fans out to many servers and engines, with a cache, a read replica, and the async filing pipeline

blocks.content:
Now a subtler bottleneck shows up: every return recomputes the **same** things. The 2024 federal tax brackets, the standard deduction amounts, each state's rate tables — these are identical for millions of users and change once a year.

A [[glossary:cache|cache]] (Redis) holds these shared tax tables and rules in memory. Instead of every calculation engine reloading the brackets from the database for every return, they read them from the cache in microseconds. The first lookup populates the cache; the next ten million are nearly free.

Cache the things that are the same for everyone — bracket tables, form definitions, rate schedules. Never cache the things that are unique and must be exact, like a specific person's income or their filed result. The line is the same one every tax engineer obsesses over: shared and slow-changing is safe to cache; personal and precise is not.

The [[node:database|database]] is still under pressure, because saving and reloading in-progress returns is constant during the interview. But that traffic is overwhelmingly **reads** — loading a return far outnumbers finalizing one.

A [[glossary:read-replica|read replica]] is a synchronized copy of the database. Servers reload in-progress returns from the replica and send the writes — saving progress, recording a filed return — to the primary. That split keeps the primary free for the writes that truly matter.

Last problem: not all the load is real filers. Some IPs hammer the site hundreds of times a second — scrapers, and your own retry logic going haywire when something is slow. Every wasted request is capacity stolen from a real person trying to beat the deadline.

[[glossary:rate-limiting|Rate limiting]] caps how many requests one client can make in a window. Cross the line and you get a `429 Too Many Requests` until you slow down.

When the worst happens and you still can't keep up, the goal becomes [[glossary:graceful-degradation|graceful degradation]]: protect the one thing that matters. Let the live refund estimate go stale, let the refund optimizer's suggestions wait, queue up filings — but never let a user's saved progress vanish or a finished return fail to record. Degrade the nice-to-haves; defend correctness to the last.

blocks.question: Why is caching the federal bracket tables safe, but caching a user's calculated refund amount dangerous?

options.text: Bracket tables are small and refunds are large
options.explanation: Size isn't the issue. A refund figure is tiny. What matters is whether the data is shared and stable, or personal and exact.

options.text: The bracket tables are identical for everyone and change once a year; a refund is unique per person and must reflect their latest inputs exactly
options.explanation: Shared, slow-changing reference data is the ideal thing to cache — compute once, serve to millions. A personal result depends on the exact numbers the user just entered, so serving a cached version risks showing someone the wrong refund.
It's a correctness problem, not a legal one. A cached refund could simply be stale — wrong the instant the user edits an input — which is reason enough never to cache it.

blocks.scenario: At 11:58 PM, a user clicks File. The load balancer happens to send their browser's automatic retry to a second app server a moment later, because the first response was slow. Now two servers are processing 'file this return' for the same return at nearly the same instant, and both ask the calculation engine to finalize and submit it.
blocks.question: How do you guarantee this return gets filed exactly once, even with two servers acting on it simultaneously?

options.text: Use a database transaction with a lock on that return so only one server can move it from 'in progress' to 'filed', and the second sees it's already filed
options.explanation: This is a classic [[glossary:race-condition|race condition]], and the database is built to resolve it. A row-level lock makes 'mark this return filed' atomic: the first server wins and transitions the return, the second finds it already filed and stops. The user files once, no matter how many servers race.

options.text: Route every File request through a single dedicated server to avoid conflicts
options.explanation: That throws away horizontal scaling at the exact moment you need it most — the deadline. The database's locking exists precisely so many servers can safely act on the same data.

options.text: Add a few seconds of delay before processing any File request so the duplicate has time to clear
options.explanation: Delays don't prevent races — both requests could still arrive within the same window, and you've made the deadline-night experience slower for everyone.

blocks.label: Deep dive: the full deadline-night path of a single return
blocks.content:
Here's what happens when a user clicks File at 11:59 PM — every component from all five stages, in order:

1. **DNS** resolves turbotax.com to the load balancer
2. **Rate limiter** checks this client hasn't blown past its request quota; if it has, it gets a `429`
3. **Auth service** confirms the session is valid (and that the user cleared 2FA earlier)
4. **Load balancer** picks a healthy app server from the fleet
5. **App server** loads the in-progress return from the **read replica**; the **workflow engine** has already walked the user to the end of the interview
6. **Calculation engine** finalizes the math, reading the shared bracket tables from the **cache** — not the database — while the **refund optimizer** has confirmed every credit is claimed
7. **PDF service** renders the official forms for the filer's records and for transmission
8. **Payment service** collects the filing fee (or it's marked to come out of the refund)
9. **App server** takes a **lock** on the return in the **primary database** and marks it filed, so a racing duplicate can't double-file
10. A filing job goes onto the **queue**; the app instantly confirms to the user
11. **Background workers** submit to the **IRS and state APIs** (falling back to the durable store if one is down), and the **email service** notifies the user when each return is accepted
12. When the refund is issued, the **bank / ACH integration** routes it to the user's account

Each layer you added across the five stages solves one specific pressure of that night. Together they turn a one-W-2 weekend project into a system that can take ten million returns in the hours before a hard, unmovable deadline.

blocks.label: Deep dive: why predictable spikes are their own kind of hard
blocks.content:
Tax season is unusual because the spike is enormous but also **known in advance** — you can see April 15 coming for a year. That changes the engineering playbook:

**Pre-scale, don't react.** You don't wait for traffic to climb and then add servers; autoscaling is too slow for a wall of traffic that arrives in minutes. You provision the fleet ahead of the deadline and tear it down afterward.

**Load-test against the peak.** Long before April, you replay synthetic deadline-night traffic at full volume to find the bottleneck that only appears at ten million returns — usually the database or a shared lock, not the servers.

**Plan the failure modes.** With a hard deadline, 'the site is slow' has legal consequences for users. So you decide in advance what to shed first (the refund-estimate preview, the optimizer's suggestions), what to queue (filings), and what must never fail (saved progress and recording a filed return).

suggestedQuestions: How far ahead of April 15 do you have to add the extra servers?
What happens to returns still on the queue at midnight — are they filed on time?
If the primary database is the bottleneck, why not just add more app servers?
